caption:
New here? Here's what JONRA does.

I help business owners get organised, get seen and grow.

That means building the processes and systems that stop the day-to-day eating your evenings, helping you win and follow up work, building websites that actually bring enquiries in, and hiring the right people first time.

Who it's for: trades, construction and property businesses, care and healthcare providers, and owner-led businesses that are busy but stuck, or growing and want to do it properly.

It starts with the Diagnostic. A recorded call, then a written report on where you are, the gaps, the quick wins and a 90-day plan.

Problems. Plan. Progress.

Tell me what's stuck. The first conversation is free. Message me. Link in bio.

Her cakes were never the problem.

Seven or eight years of home baking, all word of mouth. People loved her work. She just didn’t have the confidence to put herself out there.

So we kept it simple: her own domain, tidier socials, a routine to photograph and post every cake before it goes out, and a review card in every order.

In her words, she’s now posting more consistently, taking more pride in her work, and getting more bookings as a result.

Thank you for the 5 stars. Sometimes you just need the right person in your corner.

Got a good business but struggle with confidence or getting organised? Message me. Link in bio.

My job interview was on the way to the labour ward.

2013. Fresh out of uni, after a degree that took five years instead of three. Working double shifts, baby on the way, saving for a house.

A recruitment company called. I took the phone interview on the way to the hospital and didn't say a word.

Three days after my daughter was born, I was sat in front of the panel. I told them. They couldn't believe it. I got the job.

Character shows when it's inconvenient.

That's how I work with every client at JONRA. Message me. Link in bio.

Everyone was calling at 2pm. I called at 8pm.

In recruitment, most people rang candidates while they were at work. Busy, distracted, 30 seconds before a no.

So I flipped it. In at 7am, on the phone till 8 or 9pm, when people were home and had time to actually talk.

It still took up to 10 calls sometimes. Call one was just call one. Every call I learned something new.

Same in your business: when does your customer actually have time to talk? Start there.

“That’s not what we agreed.”

In recruitment, I never placed anyone without the terms agreed first. The rate, the hours, and on temp-to-perm deals, exactly what happened at six months. Nobody got a surprise, so there was nothing to argue about.

I bring the same thing to the businesses I work with now. Before any work starts, get three things in writing:
1. What’s included, and what isn’t
2. What it costs, and when it’s paid
3. What happens if it changes

One page, signed by both sides, saves more arguments than any conversation.

Your quote is your first impression.

I’m all about efficiency, and quoting is where a lot of owners lose their evenings. Starting from a blank page every time, retyping the same exclusions, forgetting the payment terms.

Four things that make a quote work harder:
1. Break it down: labour, materials, timescales
2. Say what’s not included
3. Put an expiry date on it
4. Follow it up within 48 hours

Then build it once as a template, so the next one takes minutes.

You don’t have to be the cheapest. You have to be the clearest, and the one who calls back.

It took ten calls before some managers took me seriously.

In recruitment I knew that going in. So call one was just call one, and I used every call to learn something: how big the team was, who used agency staff, what they were spending.

Most quotes aren’t lost on price. They’re lost because nobody followed up. A simple rhythm:
Day 2: check they got the quote
Day 7: answer the question they haven’t asked
Day 14: ask straight. Yes, no, or not yet?

A no today isn’t a no next month.

You don’t get Google reviews by hoping.

In recruitment, we visited our staff on placement with uniforms, timesheets, lunch and fruit. Other agencies’ staff told us theirs never visited, and asked to join us. Referrals were never a problem.

Reviews work the same way. Look after people properly, then make it easy for them to say so:
1. Ask at the right moment, when the job’s done and they’re happy
2. Make it one tap: a direct link or QR code
3. Put a review card in every order or invoice
4. Reply to every review

One of my clients, a home baker, now puts a review card in every order. Simple, and it works.

Your website has one job: get you the enquiry.

I build websites for trades businesses. A tape and jointing contractor came to me through a referral recently. I started on the Saturday, and they had a first draft by the Tuesday.

What a trade website needs:
1. What you do and where, in one line
2. An easy way to ask for a price or send plans
3. Click to call and WhatsApp on every page
4. Real photos and reviews

If it doesn’t bring enquiries, it’s a brochure.

Your paperwork shouldn’t live in your van.

I’m all about efficiency, and nothing wastes more time than looking for something you’ve already got. The receipt in a jacket pocket. The quote buried in a WhatsApp from March.

Three habits that fix most of it:
1. One folder per job
2. Snap receipts the same day
3. Thirty minutes in the diary every week to clear it

Set it up once and it runs itself.

5 things every quote needs:

1. An itemised price, not one number
2. What’s not included
3. Start date and how long it takes
4. Payment terms: deposit, stages, final
5. An expiry date

I’d rather send a clear quote than a cheap one. Clear quotes get fewer arguments and more yeses, and once it’s a template, the next one takes minutes.

Save this for your next quote.

Thinking about your first hire?

I spent over ten years in recruitment, placing people and leading a team of my own. Here’s what I’d sort first:
1. Know exactly what the job is
2. Write it down as a job description
3. Work out the full cost, not just the wage
4. Check they have the right to work in the UK
5. Plan their first week before they start
6. Decide how you’ll measure a good job

Then look after them. When we placed nurses, we visited them on placement with uniforms, timesheets, lunch and fruit. People stay where they feel looked after.

Hire on purpose, not in a panic.

Is your business ready to grow?

In recruitment, before I tried to grow a client, I mapped everything first: every team, who used agency staff, what they spent. Then I knew where the next bit of work was coming from.

Do the same with your own business. Tick these off honestly:
1. You know your numbers every month
2. Your prices cover your time, not just materials
3. Customers can find and contact you easily
4. Every enquiry gets followed up
5. Someone could run a day without you

Fewer than three ticks? Fix the base first.

Your 30-minute weekly business check.

When I ran a recruitment team of about ten, I didn’t tell people what to do. I showed them a format, and they mirrored it. A format is what keeps good habits going when you’re busy.

Same time, every week:
1. Money in and money out
2. Unpaid invoices chased
3. Every enquiry followed up
4. Next week’s diary planned
5. One thing improved

Small checks. Big difference. Motivation’s temporary. Consistency is the key.

Motivation gets you started. It doesn’t keep you going.

My son took up rugby years after everyone else. Not the biggest, not the fastest. He didn’t wait to feel ready. He turned up, went in for every tackle and learned the game. A few years in, he was thriving.

Myth: “I’ll start when I feel ready.”
Truth: you feel ready after you start.

Myth: “Motivated people are disciplined.”
Truth: disciplined people don’t wait for motivation.

Myth: “I’ll be consistent when things calm down.”
Truth: things calm down when you’re consistent.

Motivation’s temporary. Consistency is the key.

“Word of mouth is enough.”

Referrals were never a problem on my recruitment desk, and a recent website client came to me through a friend’s referral. So I’m a big fan.

But referrals are earned, and they slow down. Even when someone’s recommended you, they’ll Google you before they call. What do they find? A website? Reviews? Photos of your work? Or nothing?

Referrals open the door. Your website and reviews get you through it.

Busy doesn’t mean successful.

I’m all about efficiency, so when an owner tells me they’re flat out, my first question is: how much of it is the same job, done again?

Myth: “I’m flat out, so I must be doing well.”
Truth: busy can mean underpriced.

Myth: “I’ll sort the systems when it calms down.”
Truth: it calms down when you sort the systems.

Myth: “Nobody can do it like me.”
Truth: nobody can, until you show them how.

Work on the business, not just in it.
